stages.label: Early Harappan
stages.detail: Formative phase of the Indus civilisation (c. 3300-2600 BCE). Agricultural settlements spread in the Hakra-Cholistan belt, Baluchistan, and the Indus plains — building on older Neolithic roots (Mehrgarh 7000 BCE onwards). Pre-Harappan furrow at Kalibangan shows ploughing in Rajasthan. Proto-urban towns like Rahman Dheri (Baluchistan, planned roads). Mud-brick platforms, painted pottery, and female terracotta figurines foreshadow mature Harappan features. Distinct pre-Harappan layers excavated at Banawali and Kalibangan.

stages.label: Mature Harappan
stages.detail: Also called the Indus Valley Civilisation, dated c. 2600-1900 BCE. One of the earliest urban civilisations in the world, contemporaneous with Mesopotamia and Egypt. Named after Harappa, the first site discovered. Spread from Afghanistan to Gujarat. Characterised by planned cities, advanced drainage, standardised weights and seals. Sharma: extended from the Siwaliks to the Arabian Sea and from the Makran coast (Baluchistan) to Meerut — roughly 1,299,600 sq km, larger than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia. ~2800 sites identified overall; 1022 mature-phase sites (406 in Pakistan, 616 in India). Three phases: early, mature (2500-1900 BCE), late/post-urban (1900-1200 BCE). Singhania: notably no monumental temples or palaces (unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia) — suggests the civilisation was primarily mercantile rather than priest- or king-dominated.

stages.label: Late Harappan
stages.detail: Post-urban / degenerate Harappan phase (c. 1900-1300 BCE). Writing, seals, standardised weights, and monumental brickwork fall out of use. Sharma's causes: (1) Yamuna + Sutlej shifted away from Sarasvati/Hakra ~1700 BCE — water loss; (2) Elam's rise (~2000 BCE) disrupted Mesopotamia trade, cutting tin supply for bronze and bead exports; (3) rainfall decline; (4) soil exhaustion. Harappan elements persist in Gujarat (Rangpur, Rojdi), Haryana (Bhagwanpura), Punjab, and western UP (Alamgirpur). Overlaps chronologically with early Vedic migration (1500-1200 BCE) but no mass-confrontation evidence.

stages.label: Rigvedic
stages.detail: First Indo-Aryan settlement in the subcontinent (c. 1500-1000 BCE). Migration from Central Asia (Andronovo, BMAC) through Afghanistan into Sapta Sindhu — the Land of Seven Rivers (eastern Afghanistan, NWFP, Punjab, western UP fringe). Pastoral, cattle-centred society (gavishthi = "search for cows" = the term for war). Tribal assemblies: sabha, samiti, vidatha. Rig Veda composed — 10 mandalas, prayers to Agni, Indra, Mitra, Varuna. Five-tribe Panchajana; Battle of Ten Kings on Parushni (Ravi); Bharatas under Sudas emerge dominant. Priestly rivalry of Vasishtha (conservative) and Vishvamitra (liberal, composer of Gayatri). Horse (asva) mentioned 215x — marker of Aryan identity.

stages.label: Later Vedic
stages.detail: Expansion into the Ganga-Yamuna doab (c. 1000-600 BCE). Kuru-Panchala realm dominates the upper doab from Hastinapur (Meerut); Mahabharata war traditionally ~950 BCE. Iron age begins — "krishna/shyama ayas" (black metal). Painted Grey Ware culture: ~700 sites, mostly wheat-rice farming villages. Agriculture replaces pastoralism. Varna system formalises (brahmana-kshatriya-vaishya-shudra); upanayana + dvija concept emerge. Royal rituals — rajasuya (coronation), ashvamedha (territorial claim), vajapeya (chariot race). Three later Vedas composed: Sama, Yajur, Atharva. Brahmanas compiled in upper Gangetic basin. Upanishads composed ~600 BCE in Panchala + Videha — philosophical reaction against ritual excess. Jana → janapada transition: tribal identity becomes territorial polity.

stages.label: Sumerian
stages.detail: Earliest urban civilisation in southern Mesopotamia (c. 4500-2334 BCE). Sumerians invented cuneiform writing (c. 3200 BCE), the wheel, and the sexagesimal (base-60) number system that still governs our time (60 min) and angles (360°). City-states like Ur, Uruk (80,000 people by 2900 BCE), and Lagash developed on irrigation agriculture. Temple-centred social hierarchy dominated by priests. Trade connections with Meluha (Indus region) from ~2350 BCE onwards — a major source of Harappan long-distance exports.

stages.label: Akkadian
stages.detail: World's first empire (c. 2334-2154 BCE). Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian city-states from a northern base, establishing Semitic Akkadian rule over Mesopotamia. Akkadian language supplanted Sumerian as the lingua franca for centuries. Contemporaneous with the peak of mature Harappan trade. Ended with Gutian invasions from the Zagros mountains; followed by a brief Neo-Sumerian revival (Ur III, 2112-2004 BCE).

stages.label: Babylonian
stages.detail: Rose under Hammurabi (1792-1750 BCE), who unified Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule (c. 1894-1595 BCE). Code of Hammurabi — one of the earliest codified legal systems — inscribed on a stele with class-based punishments (awilum/mushkenum/wardum). Epic of Gilgamesh took its "standard" Akkadian form in this period. Ended with Kassite invasion 1595 BCE. Contemporaneous with late Harappan decline and early Vedic migration.

stages.label: Neo-Assyrian
stages.detail: Final flowering of Mesopotamian civilisation (c. 911-609 BCE). Powerful militaristic state based at Nineveh, expanding from Egypt to Persia at its peak. Overlaps with later Vedic and early Upanishadic / Mahajanapada India. Fell to a Babylonian-Median alliance — Nineveh sacked 612 BCE, empire ended 609 BCE.

nodes.label: Sargon of Akkad
nodes.detail: Founder of the Akkadian Empire (c. 2334-2279 BCE), often regarded as the first empire-builder in history. Rose from humble origins to conquer all of Sumer and expand territory from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. Established Akkad as his capital.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Rigveda
nodes.detail: The earliest composition in Sanskrit, dated to about 3500 years ago. Contains more than a thousand hymns (suktas) in praise of gods like Agni, Indra and Soma. Composed by sages and transmitted orally. Sharma: 10 mandalas (books); Books II-VII are the earliest core (family books); Books I and X are latest additions. ~1500 BCE (some parts to 1000 BCE). Collection of prayers to Agni, Indra, Mitra, Varuna etc. by various poet families. Written in Sanskrit but contains many Munda and Dravidian loanwords (from Harappan languages). Horse mentioned 215 times (most of any animal), cow 176, bull 170. Shudra varna first mentioned in Book X (the latest). Term "arya" occurs 36 times.
nodes.chapter_title: What, Where, How and When?

nodes.label: Harappan Script
nodes.detail: Remains undeciphered to this day. Written right to left with 375-400 signs, not alphabetical. Found on seals, copper tools, pottery rims, tablets, jewellery and even an ancient signboard. A bilingual inscription could help resolve the language question. Despite many attempts, scholars have not been able to decipher it. The signs are not alphabetic but logo-syllabic. First specimen noticed 1853 (Cunningham); complete script documented by 1923. ~4000 inscribed objects recovered; 250-400 pictographs. Not alphabetic — largely pictographic (each sign = a sound, idea, or object). Written right-to-left (Brahmi later left-to-right). Not deciphered; proposed links to Dravidian, Sanskrit, Sumerian — none satisfactory. Singhania: ~70% of seals bear short inscriptions in the still-undeciphered pictographic script. Writing direction is mostly right-to-left, but boustrophedon (alternating R-to-L and L-to-R on successive lines) is also attested.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Vedic Sacrificial Tradition
nodes.detail: Rigveda (c. 1500-1000 BCE) contains hymns to Agni, Indra, Soma. Sacrifices performed for cattle, sons, health. Later elaborate sacrifices like rajasuya and ashvamedha performed by kings with Brahmana priests. Upanishadic thinkers questioned the significance of sacrifices. Sharma: Rig Vedic period emphasized prayer; later Vedic period replaced prayer with elaborate sacrifices (yajna). Yajamana = sacrificer; success depended on magical power of words correctly uttered. Private (household) and public (royal) sacrifices coexisted. Cattle slaughtered on massive scale — guest was called "goghna" (fed on cattle). Rise of brahmana priests as monopolists of ritual knowledge. Reaction against sacrificial excess gave rise to the Upanishads (c. 600 BCE) in Panchala and Videha.
nodes.chapter_title: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings - Cultural Developments

nodes.label: Harappan Agriculture
nodes.detail: Crops included wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice relatively rare. Evidence of ploughed fields at Kalibangan. Irrigation through canals (Shortughai), wells and water reservoirs (Dholavira). Oxen likely used for ploughing. Crops: wheat, barley, pulses, peas, rice, sesame, linseed, mustard. Irrigation was used. Cotton was grown from about 7000 years ago at Mehrgarh. Sharma: no hoe or ploughshare found, but furrows in pre-Harappan Kalibangan show ploughing; wooden ploughs drawn by oxen (camels possibly). Stone sickles for harvest. Flood-plain sowing in November, harvest April. Gabarbands (dammed nalas) used in Baluchistan; no canal irrigation. Rice cultivated at Lothal from ~1800 BCE. Earliest cotton producers — Greeks called the area Sindon (from Sindh).
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Social Differences in Burials
nodes.detail: Objects found with skeletons suggest differences in status. At Brahmagiri, one burial had 33 gold beads while others had few pots. Megaliths with multiple skeletons indicate family burial sites with portholes for re-entry.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Earliest Cities on the Indus
nodes.detail: About 4700 years ago, some of the earliest cities in the subcontinent flourished on the banks of the Indus and its tributaries. These were the Harappan cities with planned layouts and advanced drainage.
nodes.chapter_title: What, Where, How and When?

nodes.label: Janapadas
nodes.detail: Literally 'the land where the jana set its foot and settled down'. Territorial units associated with specific peoples. Settlements included huts, cattle, and crops like rice, wheat, barley and sugarcane. Sharma: term "janapada" does NOT appear in the Rig Veda (where "jana" occurs 275 times). First appears in the Brahmanas, not earlier than 800 BCE. Marks the transition from tribal identity (jana) to territorial political unit (janapada) — tribal authority became territorial. The raja came to be called janapadin.
nodes.chapter_title: Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic

nodes.label: Standardised Bricks
nodes.detail: Bricks across all Harappan settlements maintained a standardised ratio where length and breadth were four times and twice the height respectively. Both sun-dried and baked bricks were used. This uniformity from Jammu to Gujarat indicates centralised planning. Burnt bricks were standard — in sharp contrast to Egypt (which primarily used dried bricks) and Mesopotamia (used baked bricks but far less extensively). This is one of the distinctive markers of Harappan material culture. Singhania: bricks were laid in multiple layers of well-baked brick joined with gypsum mortar. The standardised ratio (1:2:4 for thickness:width:length) was used across Harappan sites — a marker of cross-site coordination.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Sanskrit
nodes.detail: An ancient Indo-European language in which many important texts were composed including the Vedas and epics. Part of a family that includes Hindi, Persian, Greek and English.
nodes.chapter_title: What, Where, How and When?

nodes.label: Ashvamedha (Horse Sacrifice)
nodes.detail: A ritual where a horse was let loose to wander freely, guarded by the raja's men. If other rajas stopped it, they had to fight. Successful completion established the raja's supremacy over rivals. Sharma: rooted in Indo-European horse-sacrifice tradition (widespread in Europe/Central Asia from 2nd half of 5th millennium BCE). Two hymns in the 10th book of the Rig Veda; the later Vedic texts transform it into a formal royal ritual. Symbolism: the royal horse is set loose for a year, and all territory it crosses unopposed is claimed by the king — thus asserting unquestioned sovereignty over that domain.
nodes.chapter_title: Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic

nodes.label: Yajnas (Sacrifices)
nodes.detail: Rituals involving offerings of ghee, grain and sometimes animals into fire, meant for gods and goddesses. Wealth obtained from battles was used for yajnas. Performed by priests with raja as central figure. Sharma: formulae and sacrifices were invented and elaborated by the brahmanas who claimed monopoly over priestly knowledge. Performer (yajamana) attained merit through correctly uttered mantras. Dakshina (sacrificial fee) could be as much as 240,000 cows for a rajasuya — though actual transfers of land were limited despite later texts sometimes recommending the whole territory as dakshina.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Code of Hammurabi
nodes.detail: One of the oldest known written law codes, compiled c. 1754 BCE. Contains 282 laws dealing with trade, property, family, labour, and crime. Notable for its principle of lex talionis ('eye for an eye') though punishments varied by social class. Reveals a stratified society of free men, dependants, and slaves.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Akkadian Empire
nodes.detail: Founded by Sargon of Akkad c. 2334 BCE, it was the first empire in Mesopotamia unifying Sumerian and Akkadian city-states. Extended from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. Sargon is often called the first empire-builder in history. The empire lasted about 180 years.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Indo-European Language Family
nodes.detail: A family of languages including Sanskrit, Hindi, Persian, Greek, Latin and English. They share common word roots. Other Indian language families include Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman and Austro-Asiatic.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Black and Red Ware
nodes.detail: Distinctive pottery found in megalithic burials across the Deccan and south India. The dead were generally buried with these pots along with iron tools and ornaments of stone and gold.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Lower Town
nodes.detail: The eastern, larger but lower part of Harappan cities where most people lived. Houses were one or two storeys high with rooms around courtyards, separate bathing areas and wells.
nodes.chapter_title: In the Earliest Cities

nodes.label: Decline of Harappan Civilisation
nodes.detail: By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites abandoned. Marked by disappearance of seals, weights, script, long-distance trade and craft specialisation. Multiple causes proposed: climate change, deforestation, floods, river shifts. Wheeler's Aryan invasion theory challenged by George Dales in 1964. Around 1900 BCE (3900 years ago), many cities were abandoned: writing, seals and standardised weights fell out of use. Possible causes include dried rivers, deforestation, flooding, and loss of administrative control. Sharma timeline: mature phase ends ~1900 BCE; degenerate phase 1900-1500 BCE in Gujarat/Rajasthan/Haryana/western UP; post-urban 1900-1200 BCE. Causes: (1) Yamuna + Sutlej shifted away from the Sarasvati/Hakra ~1700 BCE — water loss; (2) rise of Elam ~2000 BCE interrupted Mesopotamia trade, collapsing bead/bronze crafts; (3) rainfall decline; (4) soil exhaustion; (5) some floods. No mass-confrontation evidence with Indo-Aryans.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Harappa
nodes.detail: First Harappan site to be discovered, located in Punjab (Pakistan). Badly damaged by brick robbers for railway construction. Alexander Cunningham noted it in 1875. Excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in early 20th century and R.E.M. Wheeler in 1946. Spans ~150 ha. Citadel had six granaries in two rows of six; each granary 15.23 x 6.09 m (total floor ~838 sq m). Circular brick platforms nearby for threshing — wheat and barley grains found in crevices. Two-roomed barracks likely housed labourers. Singhania finds list: stone symbol of lingam and yoni, mother goddess figurine, wheat and barley in wooden mortar, dice, copper scale and mirror, a bronze sculpture of a dog chasing a deer, and the red sandstone male torso — together establishing Harappa's rich range of art and craft artefacts.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Ur
nodes.detail: One of the most important Sumerian city-states, located in southern Mesopotamia. Flourished c. 2600-2000 BCE. Famous for its Royal Cemetery with rich grave goods, the Great Ziggurat, and as one of the world's first major urban centres. Excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s-30s.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Epic of Gilgamesh
nodes.detail: One of the earliest known works of literature, originating from Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE, compiled into an Akkadian epic c. 1200 BCE. Tells the story of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, his quest for immortality, and includes a flood narrative. Written in cuneiform on clay tablets.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Chanhudaro
nodes.detail: Small Harappan settlement of less than 7 hectares, almost exclusively devoted to craft production including bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making. Specialised drills for bead production found here. Third city of mature Harappan, about 130 km south of Mohenjo-daro in Sindh. Noted for bead-making and craft workshops.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Megaliths
nodes.detail: Large stone boulders carefully arranged to mark burial sites, beginning about 3000 years ago. Found throughout the Deccan, south India, north-east and Kashmir. Burials included Black and Red Ware pottery and iron tools.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Dholavira
nodes.detail: Major Harappan site in Kutch, Gujarat, discovered and excavated by R.S. Bisht from 1990. Entire settlement was fortified with sections separated by walls. Had elaborate water reservoirs for storing water in the arid zone. Uniquely divided into three parts with massive stone walls. Has a set of large letters carved in white stone from the Harappan script, and a large open area for ceremonies. Covers ~50 ha in Kutch (Gujarat). Stone-built citadel — most impressive Harappan citadel; dressed stone used with mud bricks in masonry. Three burial types; one has a stone circle above the grave resembling Megalithic tradition. All three Harappan phases (early, mature, late) present. Singhania: giant water reservoir; unique water-harnessing system with dams and embankments; a stadium-like structure. Inscription board comprising 10 large-sized Harappan signs — resembling an "advertisement board" (world's earliest known signboard).
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Rakhigarhi
nodes.detail: Major Harappan site in Haryana, one of the largest Harappan settlements discovered in India. Part of post-partition efforts to locate Harappan sites within Indian territory after major sites went to Pakistan. Largest Harappan site at ~250 ha — larger than Mohenjo-daro (500 ha physical size is coverage area; Rakhigarhi is comparable). Situated on the Ghaggar in Haryana. All three Harappan phases present. Singhania: granary, cemetery, drainage system, and terracotta bricks documented; confirms its status as the largest Harappan site.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Gotra System
nodes.detail: Brahmanical practice from c. 1000 BCE of classifying people by gotras named after Vedic seers. Two rules: women must adopt husband's gotra on marriage, and same-gotra marriage prohibited (exogamy). Satavahana queens retained father's gotra, showing regional variation. Sharma: literally means "cow pen" (where clan cattle were kept). The institution appeared in later Vedic times. Over time it came to signify descent from a common mythical ancestor. Gotra exogamy was enforced — marriage prohibited between persons of the same gotra.
nodes.chapter_title: Kinship, Caste and Class - Early Societies

nodes.label: Beginning of Iron Use
nodes.detail: Iron tools and weapons were found in megalithic burials including horse equipment, axes and daggers. Iron was not used in earlier Harappan cities. It enabled new agricultural and military capabilities. Sharma: pure iron first produced in Mesopotamia ~5000 BCE, Anatolia in 3rd millennium BCE. Until 1200 BCE iron was a precious metal in Western Asia. In India: Rajasthan and Karnataka in 2nd half of 2nd millennium BCE (Chalcolithic context); Gandhara by 1000 BCE; western UP by 800 BCE (arrowheads, spearheads); eastern UP by 7th century BCE. Called shyama ayas or krishna ayas ("black metal") in later Vedic texts. Iron axes enabled clearance of the Gangetic forests.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Harappan Crafts
nodes.detail: Specialists produced fine objects of copper, bronze, gold and silver. Carnelian beads were cut, shaped, polished and bored. Faience was artificially produced from sand or quartz with blue-green glaze. Singhania adds: bead factories operated at Chanhu-daro and Lothal. Beads made from carnelian, amethyst, quartz, steatite. Both men and women wore necklaces, fillets, armlets, finger rings; girdles/earrings/anklets were worn by women. Cotton and wool spun by both rich and poor — using faience (expensive) or clay (cheap) spindles/whorls.
nodes.chapter_title: In the Earliest Cities

nodes.label: Proto-Shiva Seal
nodes.detail: Seal depicting a figure seated cross-legged in yogic posture, sometimes surrounded by animals. Interpreted by some as early form of Shiva (Pashupati). However, this interpretation is debated as Rigvedic Rudra does not match this depiction. The three-horned figure sits cross-legged in yogic posture, surrounded by an elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo (below throne) and two deer (at feet). Identification as Pashupati Mahadeva is doubtful (no bull present; horned deities also appear in other ancient cultures). Phallus worship is separately attested via stone lingas at Harappa, echoed in Rigveda's reference to non-Aryan phallus-worshippers. Singhania placement detail: elephant and tiger on the left side of the figure; rhinoceros and buffalo on the right side; two antelopes shown below the seat.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Bharata Jana
nodes.detail: A group of people mentioned in the Rigveda who lived in the northwest of the subcontinent. The name Bharata was later used for the country itself.
nodes.chapter_title: What, Where, How and When?

nodes.label: Shortughai
nodes.detail: A Harappan settlement in far-off Afghanistan, established near the best source of lapis lazuli. Evidence of canals found here. Demonstrates the vast reach of Harappan trade and resource procurement networks.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Citadel
nodes.detail: The western, smaller but higher part of Harappan cities. Contained special buildings like the Great Bath and storehouses. Surrounded by walls of baked brick laid in interlocking pattern.
nodes.chapter_title: In the Earliest Cities

nodes.label: Vedic Gods: Agni, Indra, Soma
nodes.detail: Three especially important gods in the Rigveda. Agni was the god of fire, Indra was a warrior god, and Soma was a plant from which a special drink was prepared for rituals. Sharma: Indra — called Purandara (destroyer of dwelling units); has 250 hymns; warlord leading Aryans to victory; rain god. Agni — 200 hymns; the intermediary god who carries oblations as smoke to the other gods. Soma — god of plants + intoxicating drink made from a plant (likely ephedra, based on finds at Togolok-21 temple in Margiana). Many Soma-preparation hymns describe processing methods.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Harappan Burial Practices
nodes.detail: Dead generally laid in pits, some lined with bricks. Some graves contained pottery and ornaments for afterlife. Jewellery found in burials of both men and women. Overall, Harappans did not bury precious things extensively, showing relatively less social differentiation in death.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Prakrit
nodes.detail: Languages used by ordinary people in ancient India. Several forms existed, named after regions. Magadhi was the form spoken in Magadha. Used by Buddha and Mahavira for their teachings.
nodes.chapter_title: What, Where, How and When?

nodes.label: Harappan Seals
nodes.detail: Distinctive artefacts made of steatite, containing animal motifs and undeciphered script. Used to facilitate long-distance trade through sealings on goods. Script written right to left with 375-400 signs, not alphabetical. Longest inscription has about 26 signs. Generally rectangular, usually carved with an animal and the undeciphered script. The script is the earliest form of writing in the subcontinent. About 2000 seals recovered. Made of steatite or faience. Motifs: unicorns (most common), humped bull, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo, goat, elephant, antelope, crocodile. Used both as authority stamps and as amulets. Unlike Mesopotamia/Egypt, few stamped objects (sealings) survive. Singhania: shapes include square (most common), triangular, rectangular, circular. Materials: steatite (most common), agate, chert, copper, faience, terracotta, gold, ivory. Writing direction mostly right-to-left but boustrophedon (bi-directional, alternating lines) instances exist. Typical seal has animal/human figure on one side and inscription on the other; some bear inscriptions on both sides or on a third side. Motifs include unicorn, humped bull, rhinoceros, tiger, elephant, buffalo, bison, goat, markhor, ibex, crocodile, and imagined half-man-half-animal figures. Cow is notably absent. Some seals bear swastika-like symbols and mathematical-looking images. Some holed seals found with dead bodies — used as amulets.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Faience
nodes.detail: Material made of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and gum, then fired. Considered precious because difficult to make. Faience pots found mostly at Mohenjodaro and Harappa, rarely at smaller sites, indicating social stratification. An artificially produced material from sand or powdered quartz, shaped with gum and glazed to produce a shiny blue or sea-green surface. Used for beads, bangles, earrings, tiny vessels.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Harappan Drainage System
nodes.detail: Most complete ancient drainage system discovered. Streets laid out in grid pattern with drains. Every house connected to street drains through covered channels. Drains had sumps for cleaning at intervals. Found even in smaller settlements like Lothal. Covered drains laid in straight lines with gentle slopes. House drains connected to street drains, smaller feeding into larger; inspection holes at intervals for cleaning. Perhaps no other Bronze Age civilization gave drainage and public health the attention the Harappans did — no comparable system existed except arguably at Knossos (Crete). House → street drain chain, some covered with brick, some with stone slabs.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Vedic Society
nodes.detail: Society described in the Rigveda with brahmins performing rituals and rajas who were not hereditary rulers. People were called jana or vish. Battles were fought for cattle, land and water. Wealth distributed through yajnas. Sharma: Aryans divided into five tribes (panchajana). The Bharatas and Tritsu (supported by priest Vasishtha) were the dominant clans. The Battle of Ten Kings (Dasarajna) on the river Parushni (modern Ravi) established Bharata supremacy under Sudas against a coalition of ten chiefs (five Aryan, five non-Aryan); the defeated Purus later merged with Bharatas to form the Kurus, who combined with Panchalas and dominated the upper Gangetic basin in later Vedic times. Country name Bharatavarsha = derived from the Bharata tribe, first mentioned in the Rig Veda.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Babylonian Empire
nodes.detail: Centred on the city of Babylon on the Euphrates. The Old Babylonian period (c. 1894-1595 BCE) under Hammurabi unified Mesopotamia. The Neo-Babylonian Empire (626-539 BCE) under Nebuchadnezzar II built the Hanging Gardens and the Ishtar Gate. Fell to the Persian Achaemenids.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Inamgaon
nodes.detail: A site on the river Ghod, tributary of the Bhima, occupied between 3600 and 2700 years ago. Adults were buried with food vessels. One man was buried in a large four-legged clay jar in the largest house.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Vedic Rajas
nodes.detail: Early rulers mentioned in the Rigveda who did not have capital cities, palaces or armies, nor did they collect taxes. Sons did not automatically succeed fathers. They were chosen by jana for their bravery. Sharma: Rig Vedic rajan was tribal chief, largely hereditary but subject to election by samiti (assembly). Assisted by purohita (priest — Vasishtha, Vishvamitra), senani (commander), vrajapati (pasture officer), kulapa (family head), gramani (village/military head). No standing army — militia raised in wartime. In later Vedic times, vidatha disappeared; sabha/samiti survived but no longer admitted women. King performed rajasuya (coronation), ashvamedha (territorial claim), vajapeya (chariot race) to legitimize power. New officer sangrihitri collected taxes.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Harappan Craft Production
nodes.detail: Specialised craft centres existed at sites like Chanhudaro (bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making). Materials included carnelian, jasper, steatite, copper, bronze, gold, shell, faience and terracotta. Nageshwar and Balakot specialised in shell objects.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Harappan Long-Distance Trade
nodes.detail: Extensive trade network with Mesopotamia, Oman (Magan) and Bahrain (Dilmun). Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha (possibly Harappan region) and its products: carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, wood. Harappan jars found at Omani sites. Copper from Oman had nickel traces matching Harappan artefacts. NCERT raw-material sourcing: copper from Rajasthan and Oman, tin from Afghanistan and Iran, gold from Karnataka, precious stones from Gujarat, Iran and Afghanistan. Mesopotamian records from ~2350 BCE onwards refer to Meluha (= Indus region) with intermediate trading stations Dilmun (Bahrain) and Makan/Magan. No metal money — barter. Trading colony established in northern Afghanistan (Shortughai) for Central Asian trade. Used bullock-carts with solid wheels (ekka-like, not spoked).
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Painted Grey Ware
nodes.detail: A special type of pottery found at janapada sites. Grey pots with painted designs of simple lines and geometric patterns, extremely fine to touch with smooth surface. Used for special occasions. Sharma: ~700 PGW sites identified in upper Gangetic basin (western UP, Delhi, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan/Matsya), dated c. 1000-500 BCE. Bowls and dishes; used by emerging upper orders for rituals or eating. Alongside PGW the later Vedic period used three other wares: black-and-red ware, black-slipped ware, and red-ware (most popular). PGW overlaps with late Harappan pottery at Bhagwanpura (Haryana).
nodes.chapter_title: Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic

nodes.label: Great Bath
nodes.detail: Large rectangular tank in the Citadel of Mohenjodaro, made watertight with bricks set on edge and gypsum mortar. Two flights of steps on north and south. Scholars suggest it was used for special ritual bathing. Lined with bricks, coated with plaster, and made watertight with natural tar. Had steps on two sides and rooms on all sides. Dimensions: 11.88 x 7.01 m, 2.43 m deep. Burnt-brick floor; water drawn from an adjacent well; outlet from a corner to a drain. Dholavira has a comparable large tank likely used for similar ritual purpose.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Mohenjodaro
nodes.detail: The best-known Harappan site, located in Sind (present-day Pakistan). Divided into Citadel and Lower Town. Featured the Great Bath, warehouse, planned drainage system, and about 700 wells. A planned urban centre covering 125 hectares. Famous for the stone statue of a "priest-king"; houses were planned around courtyards, with covered drains. Covers ~500 ha. Name literally means "mound of the dead". Largest building is a granary 45.71 x 15.23 m. Ancient massive floods destroyed a large part of the city. Excavated by R.D. Banerjee (initial), Marshall (1931), Mackay (1938). Singhania: post-cremation burial practice also attested here; steatite Priest-King bust and bronze Dancing Girl both excavated from Mohenjo-daro. Pashupati seal found here.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Ziggurat
nodes.detail: Massive stepped pyramid temple-towers built in ancient Mesopotamia. Served as religious centres dedicated to the patron deity of the city. The most famous is the Great Ziggurat of Ur. Made of mud-brick with baked brick facing. Symbolised a connection between earth and heaven.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Harappan Weights System
nodes.detail: Precise system using cubical chert stones with no markings. Lower denominations were binary (1,2,4,8,16,32 up to 12,800), higher followed decimal system. Standardised across the entire civilisation, indicating unified authority. Base-16 system: 16, 64, 160, 320, 640 (the 16-anna rupee survived in India until recently). A bronze measuring stick with measure marks has also been found.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Hammurabi
nodes.detail: King of Babylon (r. c. 1792-1750 BCE) who unified much of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule. Famous for his law code, one of the earliest written legal codes, inscribed on a black stone stele. The code included 282 laws covering property, trade, family, and criminal matters with varying penalties by social class.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Kalibangan
nodes.detail: Harappan site in Rajasthan excavated by B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar from 1960. Evidence of ploughed field with two sets of furrows at right angles in Early Harappan levels. Also had fire altars suggesting ritual practices. Had fire altars where sacrifices may have been performed — unique among major Harappan sites. Located in northern Rajasthan; name means "black bangles". Fire altars unique to the site. Pre-Harappan furrow evidence indicates ploughing. Many houses had their own wells. Singhania: decorated bricks; bangle factory; toy carts; camel bones; citadel + lower town arrangement. Confirmed fire altar.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Brahmagiri
nodes.detail: A megalithic site where one skeleton was buried with 33 gold beads, 2 stone beads, 4 copper bangles and a conch shell, while others had only a few pots. Shows early social stratification.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: The Vedas
nodes.detail: Four sacred texts: Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. The Rigveda is the oldest, composed about 3500 years ago, containing over 1000 hymns (suktas) in Vedic Sanskrit praising gods like Agni, Indra and Soma. Sharma: four Samhitas — Rig Veda (oldest, prayers), Sama Veda (Rig prayers set to tune for recitation), Yajur Veda (hymns + rituals), Atharva Veda (charms and spells; reflects non-Aryan tradition). Each Samhita was followed by associated Brahmanas (ritualistic commentary). All later Vedic texts compiled in the upper Gangetic basin between 1000-500 BCE.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Lothal
nodes.detail: Harappan site in Gujarat, near sources of carnelian, steatite and metal. Entire settlement was fortified. Citadel was not walled off but built at a height. Had specialised bead drills and fire altars. Houses were built of mud bricks but drains of burnt bricks. Located beside a tributary of the Sabarmati near the Gulf of Khambat. Had a dockyard and a bead-making workshop; important centre for stone, shell and metal objects. Located at the head of the Gulf of Cambay in Gujarat. Rice cultivation from ~1800 BCE — unique among Harappan sites. Doubtful terracotta horse figurine. Dockyard + bead-making workshop. Singhania: nicknamed the "Manchester of the Indus Valley". Finds include a terracotta horse figurine, terracotta ship, modern-chess-like pieces, and instruments for measuring 45°, 90°, and 180° angles. Practised burial of cremated remains. Fire altars and a painted jar also recovered. A bead factory operated here.
nodes.chapter_title: Bricks, Beads and Bones - The Harappan Civilisation

nodes.label: Aryas and Dasas
nodes.detail: The Rigveda composers called themselves Aryas and their opponents Dasas or Dasyus, who did not perform sacrifices and spoke different languages. Later dasa came to mean slave, people captured in war. Sharma: Dasas appear in ancient Iranian literature too — likely a branch of early Aryans themselves (the term features in the name Divodasa, an Aryan chief). Dasyus were the original Indian inhabitants; "dasyuhatya" (slaughter of dasyus) is a repeated Rigvedic phrase. Dasyus worshipped the phallus and did not husband cattle for dairy — a key cultural divider. Trasadasyu = Aryan chief famed for overpowering dasyus.
nodes.chapter_title: What Books and Burials Tell Us

nodes.label: Assyrian Empire
nodes.detail: Powerful Mesopotamian empire centred in northern Iraq. The Neo-Assyrian Empire (911-609 BCE) was the largest empire the world had seen at its time, stretching from Egypt to Iran. Known for military prowess, administrative efficiency, and the great library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Mesopotamia
nodes.detail: Region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers (modern Iraq). One of the earliest sites of urbanisation and writing. Successive civilisations including Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians flourished here. Name means 'land between the rivers' in Greek.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Sumerians
nodes.detail: The earliest known civilisation in southern Mesopotamia (c. 4500-1900 BCE). Invented cuneiform writing, the wheel, and the sexagesimal (base-60) number system. Built city-states like Ur, Uruk, and Lagash. Developed irrigation agriculture in an arid landscape.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Cuneiform Writing
nodes.detail: One of the earliest known writing systems, developed by Sumerians around 3200 BCE. Written on clay tablets using a wedge-shaped reed stylus. Initially pictographic, it evolved into a syllabic script. Used for record-keeping, literature, law, and diplomacy for over 3,000 years.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Mesopotamian Urbanisation
nodes.detail: Among the world's first urban centres, Mesopotamian cities emerged around 4000-3000 BCE. Cities like Ur and Uruk had populations exceeding 40,000. Urbanisation was enabled by agricultural surplus from irrigation, specialisation of labour, and trade networks.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Uruk
nodes.detail: Sumerian city-state that may have been the world's first true city, with a population of up to 80,000 by 2900 BCE. Centre of the earliest known writing. Associated with the legendary king Gilgamesh. Had monumental architecture including temples and the White Temple.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Mesopotamian Irrigation
nodes.detail: Southern Mesopotamia received insufficient rainfall for farming, making irrigation essential. Elaborate canal systems diverted water from the Tigris and Euphrates. Required communal labour and central coordination, which contributed to the development of state authority and social hierarchy.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Mesopotamian Trade
nodes.detail: Mesopotamia lacked key resources like stone, metals, and timber, driving extensive long-distance trade. Traded with the Indus Valley (Meluhha), Dilmun (Bahrain), and Magan (Oman). Exported textiles and grain in exchange for metals, stones, and luxury goods. This trade fostered cultural exchange.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Mesopotamian Social Hierarchy
nodes.detail: Society was stratified into free citizens (awilum), dependants (mushkenum), and slaves (wardum). Priests and kings held highest status. Scribes formed an educated elite. Women had some property rights in earlier periods but their status declined over time. Code of Hammurabi codified class-based punishments.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Clay Tablets
nodes.detail: Primary writing medium in Mesopotamia. Made of wet clay inscribed with cuneiform using a reed stylus, then dried or baked. Hundreds of thousands have survived, preserving administrative records, letters, literature, and school texts. The durability of clay has given us an unparalleled record of ancient life.
nodes.chapter_title: Writing and City Life

nodes.label: Banawali
nodes.detail: Harappan city in Hissar district, Haryana. Contains two cultural phases — pre-Harappan and Harappan — similar to Kalibangan. Pre-Harappan features include mud-brick platforms, streets, and drains. Substantial barley discovery. Singhania: on the dried-up Sarasvati; finds include a toy plough, lapis lazuli, fire altars, barley grains. Oval-shaped settlement and the only known Harappan city with radial streets.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Surkotada
nodes.detail: Harappan site in west Gujarat with a citadel. Controversial: claimed horse remains dated c. 2000 BCE — one of the few direct (though disputed) pieces of evidence for the horse in Harappan culture. Most scholars regard the identification as uncertain. A sling-stone heap and soldier depiction on a potsherd hint at a possible standing force.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Sutkagendor
nodes.detail: Coastal Harappan city in Baluchistan (Pakistan), on the Makran coast. Marked by a citadel; served as a maritime outpost for long-distance trade with Mesopotamia via the Arabian Sea.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Meluha
nodes.detail: Ancient Mesopotamian name for the Indus region (from ~2350 BCE onwards in cuneiform records). Mesopotamian texts record trade with Meluha in carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, and wood. The identification with the Harappan civilisation is near-universally accepted — a cornerstone piece of evidence for direct Indus-Mesopotamia commerce.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Dilmun
nodes.detail: Ancient trading station identified with modern Bahrain in the Persian Gulf. Intermediate between Mesopotamia and Meluha (Indus). Mesopotamian texts describe it as a transshipment point; thousands of graves survive awaiting excavation.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Magan / Makan
nodes.detail: Ancient trading station, between Dilmun and Meluha. Generally identified with modern Oman (also called Makan in Sharma). Source of copper that reached Mesopotamia; nickel traces in Harappan copper artefacts match Omani sources, confirming the trade link.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Dancing Girl
nodes.detail: Bronze figurine recovered from Mohenjo-daro — one of the finest specimens of Harappan metal art. Naked, wears a necklace and bangles on one arm, right hand on hip, head tilted back. Demonstrates advanced lost-wax casting technique. UPSC PYQ 2025: the figurine is made of BRONZE. Singhania: the world's oldest known bronze sculpture (~4 inches / 10.5 cm tall). Stands in a "tribhanga" (three-bends) dancing posture, right hand on hip, head tilted slightly. Ornamented with bangles on the left arm and an amulet + bracelet on the right arm. Cast via the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Priest-King Sculpture
nodes.detail: Steatite bust from Mohenjo-daro. Wears an ornamented robe passing over the left shoulder under the right arm like a shawl; short hair locks at the back are held by a woven fillet. Marshall nicknamed it the "priest-king", but the identification is speculative — there is no evidence of priest-rule in Harappan civilisation. Singhania: the steatite figure shows a bearded man draped in a shawl with trefoil patterns. Eyes are elongated and half-closed, as if in meditation. Armlet on the right hand, plain woven fillet tied across the head. Marshall's label "priest-king" is speculative.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Sarasvati / Hakra-Ghaggar
nodes.detail: The ancient Sarasvati is identified with the Hakra-Ghaggar river system (now largely dried up). In the third millennium BCE, the Yamuna and Sutlej flowed into it due to Himalayan tectonic shifts, creating a major water source supporting many Harappan sites. Around 1700 BCE both tributaries shifted away, drying up the Sarasvati — a major contributor to Harappan decline. Some scholars call the civilisation the "Sarasvati culture" for this reason.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Elam
nodes.detail: Ancient state on the eastern border of Mesopotamia (covering much of Iran). Its rise around 2000 BCE disrupted the long-distance trade between the Indus region and Mesopotamia — cutting off tin supply to Harappan bronze-workers and bead/luxury exports to Mesopotamia. A major factor in Harappan urban decline.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Culture: Bronze Age Urbanization in the Indus Valley

nodes.label: Sama Veda
nodes.detail: The second Veda — Rig Vedic prayers set to melody ("saman") for ritual recitation. One of the four Samhitas. Considered the source of Indian music traditions (musical scales derived from saman chants).
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Yajur Veda
nodes.detail: The third Veda. Contains not only hymns but also the prose formulae (yajus) that accompany rituals — reflecting the elaboration of sacrifice in the later Vedic period. Divided into Shukla (white/Vajasaneyi) and Krishna (black) recensions.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Atharva Veda
nodes.detail: The fourth Veda. Contains charms and spells to ward off evil and disease. Reflects a strong non-Aryan / folk tradition — often considered to have absorbed indigenous pre-Aryan practices. Also contains early speculation on philosophical and medical themes.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Brahmanas (Texts)
nodes.detail: Prose texts attached to each Veda that explain the ritual and its symbolism. Compiled in the upper Gangetic basin c. 1000-500 BCE. Major examples: Shatapatha Brahmana (Yajur), Aitareya Brahmana (Rig). First use of the term "janapada" (c. 800 BCE).
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Andronovo Culture
nodes.detail: Bronze Age archaeological culture covering almost the whole of Central Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE. Considered proto-Indo-Iranian: characterised by stock-breeding, widespread horse use, spoked-wheel chariots, cremation, pit-dwellings roofed with birch, and the soma drink. Likely ancestral cultural zone of the Vedic Aryans who migrated to India.
nodes.chapter_title: Identity of Aryan Culture

nodes.label: Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC)
nodes.detail: Archaeological complex covering south Central Asia (Bactria/Afghanistan + Margiana/Turkmenistan+Uzbekistan), c. 1900-1500 BCE. Shows evidence of domestic horse, spoked-wheel chariots, partial cremation, and svastika motif by 1500 BCE. The migratory herdsmen who damaged its proto-urban settlements may have moved to the Indian subcontinent's borders — consistent with horse remains + post-cremation burials appearing in the Swat valley from c. 1400 BCE.
nodes.chapter_title: Identity of Aryan Culture

nodes.label: Indo-Aryan Migration
nodes.detail: Migration of Indo-Aryans into the Indian subcontinent from Central Asia, in several waves beginning c. 1500-1200 BCE. Evidence: genetic marker M17 present in 40%+ of Central Asian steppe populations and 35% of Hindi speakers (vs 10% of Dravidian speakers); linguistic links with Russian; archaeological trail through Andronovo and BMAC cultures. No inscriptional Indo-Aryan evidence survives in India itself from this period — all Indo-European inscriptions from this era come from West Asia (Kassite, Mitanni, Hittite).
nodes.chapter_title: Identity of Aryan Culture

nodes.label: Sapta Sindhu (Land of Seven Rivers)
nodes.detail: Land of the Seven Rivers — the area where the Aryans first settled in the subcontinent, covering eastern Afghanistan, the North-West Frontier Province, Punjab, and fringes of western UP. The seven rivers centre on the Sindhu (Indus) and its five tributaries, plus the Sarasvati (Rig Vedic naditama, "best of rivers") which was identified variously with the Hakra-Ghaggar or the Avestan Harakhwati (Helmand, in south Afghanistan).
nodes.chapter_title: The Age of the Rig Veda

nodes.label: Battle of Ten Kings (Dasarajna)
nodes.detail: Key conflict described in the Rig Veda. Fought on the river Parushni (modern Ravi) between the Bharatas (under king Sudas, supported by priest Vasishtha) and a coalition of ten chiefs — five Aryan tribes and five non-Aryan peoples. Bharatas won, establishing their supremacy. The defeated Purus later merged with Bharatas to form the Kurus.
nodes.chapter_title: The Age of the Rig Veda

nodes.label: Bharatas
nodes.detail: Dominant Aryan ruling clan of the Rig Vedic period, first mentioned in the Rig Veda. Victorious at the Battle of Ten Kings under Sudas. Merged with the defeated Purus to form the Kurus. Source of the name "Bharatavarsha" for the Indian subcontinent.
nodes.chapter_title: The Age of the Rig Veda

nodes.label: Kurus
nodes.detail: Later Vedic ruling tribe formed by the merger of Bharatas and Purus. Initially settled between Sarasvati and Drishadvati, then occupied Delhi and the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab ("Kurukshetra"). Coalesced with Panchalas to form the dominant Kuru-Panchala realm. Mahabharata war (~950 BCE) fought between Kauravas and Pandavas — both Kuru branches.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Panchalas
nodes.detail: Later Vedic tribe occupying the central Ganga-Yamuna doab (modern Bareilly, Badaun, Farrukhabad districts). Famous for its philosopher-kings and brahmana theologians. Combined with Kurus to form the Kuru-Panchala realm. Panchala (and Videha) was the home of the Upanishadic tradition c. 600 BCE.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Hastinapur
nodes.detail: Capital of the Kuru-Panchala realm in later Vedic times, situated in Meerut district (western UP). Archaeologically dated 900-500 BCE — shows early settlement and faint beginnings of town life (proto-urban). Tradition says it was flooded and the Kurus moved to Kaushambi near Allahabad. Central setting of the Mahabharata narrative.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Mahabharata War
nodes.detail: War between the Kauravas (Duryodhana's faction) and Pandavas (Yudhishthira's faction) — both branches of the Kuru clan — for succession to the throne of Hastinapur. Traditionally dated c. 950 BCE; the epic was finally compiled c. 4th century CE. The war effectively wiped out the Kuru ruling clan.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Vasishtha
nodes.detail: Conservative priestly sage of the Rig Vedic period. Author of many hymns (mandala VII is traditionally attributed to him and his family). Supported the Bharata ruler Sudas at the Battle of Ten Kings. Traditional rival of Vishvamitra.
nodes.chapter_title: The Age of the Rig Veda

nodes.label: Vishvamitra
nodes.detail: Liberal Rig Vedic sage, traditionally a kshatriya who attained brahmana status through ascetic achievement. Composer of the Gayatri mantra (Rig Veda 3.62.10) which was conceived as a universal admission formula to the Aryan fold — though later priests restricted it to the three upper varnas only. Mandala III of the Rig Veda is traditionally attributed to him and his family.
nodes.chapter_title: The Age of the Rig Veda

nodes.label: Gayatri Mantra
nodes.detail: A Rig Vedic verse (3.62.10) composed by Vishvamitra. Intended originally as a universal admission mantra into the Aryan fold. Later priests made it the exclusive privilege of the three upper varnas (brahmanas, kshatriyas, vaishyas) — shudras and women were prohibited from reciting it.
nodes.chapter_title: The Age of the Rig Veda

nodes.label: Rajasuya
nodes.detail: Royal coronation sacrifice of later Vedic times. Supposed to confer supreme power on the king. Accompanied by large-scale dakshina (sacrificial fee) — traditionally 240,000 cows. One of the three major royal rituals alongside Ashvamedha and Vajapeya.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Vajapeya
nodes.detail: Later Vedic royal ritual involving a chariot race in which the king's chariot was made to "win" against his kinsmen's. Reinforced the king's ritual supremacy. Cognate with Greek and Indo-European chariot-race traditions, suggesting deep Indo-European antiquity.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Prajapati
nodes.detail: The creator god who rose to supreme position in the later Vedic pantheon, displacing Rig Vedic Indra and Agni. Associated with the ritual of creation through sacrifice.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Rudra
nodes.detail: The god of animals in later Vedic texts. Minor in the Rig Veda, rose in later Vedic times. Later identified with Shiva — a continuity from Rig Veda's Rudra into the later Puranic Shiva.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Vishnu (Early Vedic form)
nodes.detail: Minor solar deity in the Rig Veda, known for the three strides covering the universe. In later Vedic times, came to be conceived as preserver and protector of settled people. This pattern evolves into the major Puranic Vishnu of post-Vedic Hinduism.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Upanayana (Sacred Thread)
nodes.detail: Rite of investiture with the sacred thread (yajnopavita), marking the beginning of Vedic education. Entitlement of the three higher varnas (brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya) — known collectively as dvija (twice-born). Shudras and women were barred. The rite marked entry into the brahmacharya ashrama (student stage).
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Dvija (Twice-Born)
nodes.detail: Term for the three upper varnas (brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya) — those entitled to upanayana (sacred thread) and therefore to Vedic study. Shudras and women were excluded. The concept formalized the religious hierarchy of the varna system.
nodes.chapter_title: The Later Vedic Phase

nodes.label: Sabha and Samiti
nodes.detail: Tribal assemblies of the Rig Vedic period. Sabha was a smaller council (possibly of elders/nobles); samiti was a larger popular assembly with deliberative, military, and religious functions. Even women attended in early Vedic times. In later Vedic times, vidatha disappeared, and sabha/samiti became dominated by warriors and brahmanas — women were barred.
nodes.chapter_title: The Age of the Rig Veda

nodes.label: Ropar
nodes.detail: Harappan site on the banks of the Sutlej in Punjab (India). Distinctive find: a dog buried with a human in oval pit burials — unique evidence of human-dog companionship in burial practice. Copper axe also recovered.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Art and Architecture

nodes.label: Alamgirpur
nodes.detail: Easternmost known site of the Indus Valley Civilisation, in Meerut district (western UP) on the Yamuna. Finds: broken copper blade, ceramic items, and impression of cloth on a trough (evidence of cotton textile use in the late Harappan phase).
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Art and Architecture

nodes.label: Lost-Wax Bronze Casting (Cire Perdue)
nodes.detail: Ancient bronze-casting technique used by Harappan metalsmiths to produce the Dancing Girl and other figurines. Process: a wax figure is coated with clay; the clay is baked, melting out the wax; molten metal is poured into the hollow mould; after solidifying, the clay is broken away to reveal the metal figure. Still practised in parts of India (e.g. Dhokra craft of West Bengal/Odisha/Chhattisgarh).
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Art and Architecture

nodes.label: Mother Goddess Figurine
nodes.detail: Terracotta female figurines found at many Harappan sites. Standing female adorned with necklaces over prominent breasts, a loincloth with girdle, and a distinctive fan-shaped headgear. Crudely modelled — made by pinching. Likely worshipped for prosperity and fertility — evidence of an early mother-goddess / fertility cult.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Art and Architecture

nodes.label: Red Sandstone Male Torso
nodes.detail: A rock sculpture found at Harappa. Frontal posture; well-baked shoulders and a prominent abdomen. Socket holes in the neck and shoulders suggest the head and arms were made separately and attached. Notable for its sophistication compared to the simpler Mohenjo-daro Priest-King figure.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Art and Architecture

nodes.label: Harappan Painted (Red and Black) Pottery
nodes.detail: Distinctive Harappan pottery featuring a red slip background with glossy black designs — trees, birds, animals, geometric patterns. Mostly wheel-made; rare handmade pieces. Also rare polychrome examples. Perforated pottery (large bottom hole, small side holes) likely used for straining liquor. Miniature vessels (<half-inch) exquisitely crafted for decoration. Distinct from later Vedic Black-and-Red Ware.
nodes.chapter_title: Harappan Art and Architecture
